## The same seven steps, every time

::: steps
<div><b>Question</b>what you want to know, sharp enough to answer</div>
<div><b>Data</b>where it comes from, what it can't tell you</div>
<div><b>Cleaning</b>from raw to usable, every step in code</div>
<div><b>Exploration</b>look before you test</div>
<div><b>Analysis</b>the comparison, model or test</div>
<div><b>Conclusions</b>what follows, and its limits</div>
<div><b>Reproduce</b>one command, same numbers</div>
:::

<p style="margin-top:1.4em">This is the <b>data science life cycle</b>. It is also the seven sections of every report you will write in this course.</p>

::: notes
Keep this slide in mind: every project that follows is told along these seven steps.
:::

# Are baby names a fashion? {.divider}

<p class="muted">Small project · one source</p>

## Names skip three generations

<img src="/img/introduction/names-comebacks.svg" alt="Share of births named Elsa, Alice and Astrid, 1922–2021: high in the 1920s, almost zero in 1960–80, high again after 2000">

<p class="small">Share of each birth year with the name, among the 200 most common names in Sweden. Data: SCB.</p>

::: notes
Common in the 1920s, nearly gone around 1970 (grey band), back after 2000. Ask: who in the room
has a grandmother or great-grandmother called Elsa, Alice or Astrid?
:::

## The catch: only the living are counted

- The table counts people **alive in Sweden in 2021**, by year of birth.
- Someone born in 1925 who has died or emigrated is not in it.
- And it only lists names that are common **today**: a 1925 name that never came back is missing.

<div class="callout">The data is tilted towards finding comebacks. Saying so is part of the result.</div>

::: notes
Survivorship bias. This is the step where the real thinking was in this project: the
conclusion and its limitation. A small project with an honest limitation is a good project.
:::

```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/lifecycle-names.svg >}}
```

<p class="small muted">One source, one straight line. The red step is where the work was. <a href="https://github.com/su-mt4008/lecture-demos/tree/main/introduction/names">The report on GitHub</a></p>

# Why does electricity cost more in Malmö than in Luleå? {.divider}

<p class="muted">Medium project · two sources joined</p>

## Four zones, one country

<img src="/img/introduction/electricity-zones.svg" alt="Monthly mean spot price in SE4 Malmö and SE1 Luleå, 2023–2025; Malmö is above Luleå almost every month">

<p class="small">Monthly mean spot price, 2023–2025. Data: Nord Pool via elprisetjustnu.se.</p>

::: notes
Sweden has four price zones since 2011. The gap is the shaded area. Question: how big is it,
and does it go with the weather? Wind power in the south should push southern prices down.
:::

## Where the work was: cleaning

- Prices per **hour**, then per **15 minutes** from October 2025: a plain mean weighs them wrongly.
- Clocks change twice a year: some days have **23 or 25 hours**.
- Prices are in UTC, weather in Swedish dates: join on the **right** day.
- **22 of 1,096 days** have no weather data. Dropped, and reported.

<div class="callout">None of this shows in the final figure. All of it changes the numbers if done wrong.</div>

::: notes
This is what joining sources really means. Each bullet is a bug that would silently shift
the result. The rendered report shows every one of these steps in code.
:::

## Calm days, big gap

<img src="/img/introduction/electricity-wind.svg" alt="Mean price gap by wind quarter: 0.55 SEK per kWh on the calmest days, falling to 0.15 on the windiest">

On calm days Malmö pays **0.40 kr/kWh more** than on windy days (95% interval 0.34 to 0.47). But wind and temperature explain only **18%** of the day-to-day gap.

::: notes
The interval is a bootstrap, which you will see in the second half. The 18%: the rest is the
grid, nuclear maintenance and continental prices, which this data doesn't contain.
Correlation, not cause: windy days also differ in season and demand.
:::

# Is AI a bubble? {.divider}

<p class="muted">Ambitious project · three sources, and a question that needs work first</p>

## You can't measure a bubble

So turn the question into things you **can** measure.

| A bubble means … | We measure | Source |
|:--|:--|:--|
| prices far above what companies earn | price / earnings over 10 years (CAPE) | Shiller, since 1871 |
| prices that rose unusually fast | NASDAQ compared with 5 years earlier | FRED |
| everybody talking about it | share of Hacker News titles saying "AI" | HN Search API |

<p class="small muted">The question becomes: how do today's values compare with 1929, 2000 and the crypto boom?</p>

::: notes
This is the step that makes it an A-level project: operationalising. The data can't say
"bubble"; it can say how unusual today is on signs that people associate with bubbles.
:::

## Valuations: second only to 2000

<img src="/img/introduction/ai-cape.svg" alt="Cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio of US stocks since 1881, with 1929, 2000 and today marked; today is above 1929 and just below 2000">

<p class="small">CAPE of the S&P composite. Data: Robert Shiller.</p>

::: notes
Only the months around the 2000 peak were higher. 1929 was lower than today.
A cleaning trap: Shiller writes October as 2026.1, which as a number is the same as January.
:::

## Prices: an ordinary pace

<img src="/img/introduction/ai-nasdaq.svg" alt="NASDAQ divided by its value five years earlier, since 1976; the 2000 peak is far higher than today">

<p class="small">The NASDAQ index divided by its value five years earlier. Data: FRED.</p>

<p>Today ×1.6: higher than only <b>40%</b> of months. In 2000: ×5.9. <span class="accent">This sign is not there.</span></p>

::: notes
This is the slide that makes the project honest. Showing only CAPE and attention would make a
more exciting story and a less true one. Report the evidence that goes against you.
:::

## Attention: four times the crypto peak

<img src="/img/introduction/ai-attention.svg" alt="Share of Hacker News story titles mentioning AI, bitcoin and crypto, 2007 to today; AI is far above the earlier crypto peaks">

<p class="small">Share of Hacker News story titles with each word, 3-month average. Data: HN Search API.</p>

## The honest answer

<p class="big">Two of three signs that came before earlier crashes are there.<br>Whether a crash follows is <span class="accent">not in the data</span>.</p>

- High valuations can last for years; if AI raises earnings as expected, prices may be right.
- Three signs is our choice. US data, an English-language forum, few past bubbles to compare.

::: notes
An A is not about a bigger dataset. It's about a question that takes real effort, results
that are checked, and conclusions that would convince a sceptical reader, including what you
can't conclude.
:::

# How the course works {.divider}

## What this course is

Data science is the whole cycle: from a question, through messy real data, to an answer someone else can **check**. Statistics is how you know how sure you can be; code is how you make it repeatable.

- **Tools:** Python or R, Quarto, Git and GitHub, VS Code. You choose the language.
- **Six weeks**, one theme each: reproducible analysis · tables and plots · cleaning and exploring · joins and databases · data from the web · text as data.

<p class="more">More: <a href="/about">About the course</a></p>

- **Self-study first.** Each week's material is on the site: read it, run the code.

# Week 1: reproducible analysis {.divider}

## Can someone else get your numbers?

In 2010, an influential economics paper found that growth falls sharply when government debt passes 90% of GDP. Governments cited it.

In 2013 a student tried to **reproduce** it from the authors' spreadsheet, and found rows left out of an average. The striking result shrank to a modest one.

<div class="callout">A result nobody can reproduce is, scientifically, just a claim.</div>

::: notes
Reinhart and Rogoff (2010), "Growth in a Time of Debt"; Herndon, Ash and Pollin (2013).
The error was found because someone could rerun it. Make that possible for your own work.
:::

## Why analyses don't reproduce

| What goes wrong | The habit that prevents it |
|:--|:--|
| Different package versions | a **locked environment** |
| A variable you made by hand, then deleted the code | **render from scratch** |
| You fixed a typo in the CSV, in Excel | **never edit raw data**; change it in code |
| `C:\Users\anna\Downloads\data.csv` | **relative paths**: `data/raw/data.csv` |
| A random sample differs every run | **set a seed** |
| The data was never committed | commit it, and let **the check** catch it |

<p class="more">More: <a href="/lectures/week-1#why-reproducibility-matters">Week 1</a></p>

## Start with a question data can answer

| Vague | Answerable |
|:--|:--|
| "Look at Stockholm's weather." | Has Stockholm's mean annual temperature changed since the late 1990s? |
| "Analyse electricity prices." | How much more did southern Sweden pay than the north in 2023–25? |
| "Is AI a bubble?" | How do three signs of a bubble compare with 1929 and 2000? |

<p>A good question names <b>what</b> you measure, <b>where</b> and <b>when</b>, and what you'll <b>compare</b>.</p>

## Your repository

```
<username>-assignments/
├─ hw1/
│  ├─ report.qmd     ← your report: text and code, seven sections
│  ├─ report.md      ← the rendered report (made by Quarto)
│  └─ data/raw/      ← data exactly as you got it, with its source
├─ hw2/ … hw5/
├─ example/          ← a worked example of a report
├─ pyproject.toml + uv.lock   or   renv.lock   ← the locked environment
└─ .github/workflows/check.yml                ← the reproducibility check
```

<p class="small muted">Same structure every time: a reader knows where to look, and everything generated can be remade with one command.</p>

## Lockfiles: "works on my machine" → works on every machine

- Your code depends on packages, and packages change.
- A **lockfile** records the exact version of every package.
- Anyone can rebuild the same environment from it:

```bash
uv sync                      # Python
Rscript -e "renv::restore()" # R
```

- Add a package with `uv add pandas` or `renv::install("dplyr")` + `renv::snapshot()`. Never edit the lockfile by hand.

## Quarto: text and code in one file

````markdown
## Analysis

```{{python}}
yearly = temps.groupby("year")["temp"].mean()
yearly.loc[2011:].mean() - yearly.loc[:2010].mean()
```

The later period is warmer by 0.82 °C.
````

- `quarto render` runs the code and writes `report.md` with the results and figures.
- The numbers in your text come **from** the code, not copied by hand.

## Git: four words

- **commit**: save a snapshot, with a message saying why.
- **branch**: a separate line of work; `hw1` next to `main`.
- **push**: send your commits to GitHub.
- **pull request**: "please look at this branch": where the check runs and the review happens.

<p style="margin-top:1em">You will use these four every week. The guide has every command, for VS Code.</p>

<p class="more">More: <a href="/guide#hand-in-an-assignment">How to hand in</a></p>

## The check

When you open or update a pull request, GitHub starts a clean computer, installs your locked environment and renders your report.

- **Green:** your analysis reproduces. Anyone can get your numbers.
- **Red:** something only works on your computer. The log says what.

<p class="more">More: <a href="/guide#when-the-check-is-red">When the check is red</a></p>

# Statistics: the basics {.divider}

<p class="muted">From Probability I to statistics, in fifteen minutes.</p>

## Probability ↔ statistics

| Probability (MT3001) | Statistics (now) |
|:--|:--|
| You know the model: $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ | You have the data: $x_1, \dots, x_n$ |
| What will the data look like? | What was the model? And how sure are you? |

Data are **observations of random variables**. Your mean $\bar x$ is one value of the random variable $\bar X$: another sample would have given another value.

<p class="more">More: <a href="/statistics">Statistics: the basics</a></p>

## Our example: has Lund got warmer?

<img src="/img/statistics/data.svg" alt="Mean annual temperature in Lund, 1997–2025, with the mean of 1997–2010 and of 2011–2025">

The later period is **0.82 °C** warmer. Is that real, or could weather alone do it?

::: notes
Lund, not Stockholm: Stockholm is HW1, and we don't give away the answer.
:::

## Single years scatter a lot

<img src="/img/statistics/spread.svg" alt="Each year's mean temperature as a dot, for both periods, with mean plus and minus one standard deviation">

<p class="small">One year varies by about 0.6 °C. The difference we found is not much larger.</p>

## Means scatter much less

<img src="/img/statistics/sampling.svg" style="max-height:320px" alt="Simulated: single years scatter widely, means of 14 years scatter much less">

$$\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \operatorname{SE} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \approx \frac{0.62}{\sqrt{14}} = 0.17 \text{ °C}$$

<p class="small muted">To halve the uncertainty, you need four times the data.</p>

## Confidence intervals

By the CLT, $\bar X \approx N(\mu, \operatorname{SE}^2)$, so $\;\bar x \pm 1.96\,\operatorname{SE}\;$ covers $\mu$ in 95% of samples.

<img src="/img/statistics/intervals.svg" style="max-height:330px" alt="20 simulated 95% intervals; 19 contain the true mean, one misses">

<p class="small">"95%" is a property of the method: about 1 in 20 intervals misses.</p>

## The difference, with its uncertainty

$$\operatorname{SE}_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{\frac{s_a^2}{n_a} + \frac{s_b^2}{n_b}} = 0.23 \qquad 0.82 \pm 1.96 \cdot 0.23 = [0.37,\ 1.27] \text{ °C}$$

The whole interval is above zero: consistent with warming of 0.4 to 1.3 °C, **not** with no warming.

## The same, by computer: the bootstrap

<img src="/img/statistics/bootstrap.svg" style="max-height:330px" alt="Histogram of the difference in 10,000 resampled datasets, with the middle 95% marked">

Resample the years with replacement, 10,000 times; the middle 95% of the differences is the interval. **No formula needed**, and it works for almost any statistic.

## Could it be chance? A test

$H_0$: no difference. Then $\;z = \dfrac{0.82}{0.23} = 3.6\;$ and $\;p = P(|Z| \ge 3.6) \approx 0.0003$.

<img src="/img/statistics/permutation.svg" style="max-height:290px" alt="Differences when the years are shuffled between the periods at random; the observed difference is far in the tail">

<p class="small">By computer: shuffle the years between the periods; how often is the difference as large? About 1 in 1,000.</p>

## What a p-value is not

- **Not** the probability that $H_0$ is true.
- **Not** the size or importance of the effect: report the estimate and its interval.
- $p > 0.05$ does **not** show there is no effect: maybe too little data.

## Correlation and trend

<img src="/img/statistics/trend.svg" alt="Lund annual mean temperature with a fitted straight line">

<p>Slope <b>0.54 °C per decade</b> (95% interval 0.27 to 0.80), $r = 0.62$. Correlation is not causation: here the cause comes from physics, not from this data.</p>

## The many-tests trap

<img src="/img/statistics/many-tests.svg" style="max-height:330px" alt="20 tests on pure random noise; one has p below 0.05">

<p>Twenty tests on pure noise: one comes out "significant". Test many things and something always will. Decide what to test <b>before</b> you look.</p>

## Writing it up

<div class="callout big" style="font-size:1.1em">The years 2011–2025 were on average 0.82 °C warmer in Lund than 1997–2010 (95% confidence interval 0.37 to 1.27 °C).</div>

- The **estimate**, with **units**.
- Its **uncertainty**.
- What it does **not** show: why, or what happens next.
